meta.notes: Case data for cartridge brass. Manufacturer case weight / water capacity is only published by Peterson (per-lot QC table; "Average Internal Volume (Grains of H20)", fill point not stated). Lapua, Norma and Starline product pages publish product numbers, calibers and (Lapua, Starline) primer size, but no weight/capacity, so those fields are null. Third-party measurements come from AccurateShooter.com cartridge guides; measurement methods are recorded per record. Peterson per-lot values are verbatim; "petersonStats" is derived (min/median/max) and flagged derived. qualityFlags mark Peterson lots deviating >5% from their cartridge median (verbatim values kept); "SUSPECT" flags (>25% off the median, e.g. 375 CheyTac lot C160 listed with 59.4 gr H2O vs ~160 for all other lots) mark probable source data-entry errors, set suspectSourceValue=true and are excluded from petersonStats. Water capacity varies with lot, condition (new vs fired), chamber and fill point; never treat one record as a universal case volume. primerSize vocabulary: "small rifle", "large rifle", "small pistol", "large pistol", optional " magnum", or "X or Y" when the maker lists two options. Crawl: robots.txt of every host read first and obeyed (Starline Disallow /*?* -> no query URLs; Peterson Disallow /files/ -> PDFs skipped; AccurateShooter Disallow /wp-content/ -> nothing fetched there); >=1.5 s between requests per host; plain curl default user agent.

brands.notes: Official company name per about page: Nammo Lapua Oy (centerfire, Lapua, Finland) and Nammo Schönebeck (rimfire, Germany). Country = where centerfire components (incl. cases) are produced.
brands.evidence: Lapua, or more officially Nammo Lapua Oy and Nammo Schönebeck, is part of the large Nammo Group. Our main products are small caliber cartridges and components for sport, hunting and professional use. Lapua manufactures centerfire cartridges in Lapua, Finland, and rimfire cartridges in Schonebeck, Germany. || In 1998, the Nammo group was founded, and in the early 2000s, Nammo acquired the factory in Schönebeck, Germany, where Lapua rimfire cartridges are produced today. All Lapua centerfire components and cartridges are produced at the factory site located in Lapua, Finland. Today, hundreds of Nammo employees work with the Lapua brand at various Nammo locations. || Nammo Lapua Oy is part of Nammo group. Nammo is an international aerospace and defense company headquartered in Norway. With more than 2 700 employees, 28 production sites and a presence in 12 countries, Nammo is one of the world’s leading providers of specialty ammunition and rocket motors. || catalog heading: LAPUA® CENTERFIRE CASES

brands.name: Peterson Cartridge
productLines: Peterson rifle brass (casings), incl. small-rifle-primer (SRP) variants
brands.notes: Publishes per-lot QC data (average empty weight, average internal volume in grains of H2O) on its Ballistician Testing Data page. Technical drawings are PDFs under /files/, disallowed by robots.txt, not fetched.
brands.evidence: Founded in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania by Derek Peterson and his two business partners, Peterson Cartridge was built with one main goal. That goal is to produce extremely consistent, American-Made brass rifle casings which are designed around, and for long-distance shooters. || We are a proud member of the Peterson Brothers, Inc. team and are made with pride, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania USA. || To further our mission of creating brass for shooters by shooters, our in-house ballistician has begun providing AMP Aztec Codes from an AMP Mark II Annealer for as many of our lots as possible.

brands.name: Starline Brass
brands.notes: About page: founded 1976 (West Covina, California), relocated 1992 to Sedalia, Missouri; family-owned. No parent company stated.
brands.evidence: About Starline Brass | Made in USA Since 1976 || Starline Brass was founded in 1976 by three men with ties to Sierra Bullets: Robert Hayden, Frank Snow, and Paul Knepp, with the goal of manufacturing high-quality brass for reloading. Initially operating in West Covina, California, the company focused on custom headstamps before a large contract from the Federal Government for the FBI's newly adopted 10mm Auto cartridge fueled growth. In the early days, Robert’s wife, Barbara Hayden, ran the office and handled the accounting duties. || In 1992, Starline relocated to Sedalia, Missouri, to expand and improve distribution and escape the increasingly difficult manufacturing climate in California. || Today, Starline Brass remains a family-owned business known for its stringent quality control and broad range of calibers, serving the reloading market from its state-of-the art 60,000 square-foot Missouri facility. Barbara’s commitment to Starline Brass lives on through her family and Starline’s CEO Robert (Bobby) Hayden, Jr.

brands.name: IMI Match
brands.notes: Headstamp named in a third-party (AccurateShooter.com) measurement table; no maker page consulted, so country/parent are not stated.
brands.evidence: The most important thing to remember about military brass is that the internal capacity will probably be less than commercial .308 Win brass, because military brass often has thicker webs or casewalls. Montana Marine reports his fire-formed milsurp cases hold 56 grains of H20 on average compared to 58 grains for fire-formed Winchester. Given the reduced capacity of military brass, you should reduce posted max loads by 1.5 grains when loading with Lake City or most other milsurp brass. However, the IMI MATCH brass is closer to commercial brass in internal case capacity (ICC). Kevin Beggs reports: “Fired, my IMI Match brass runs with an ICC of 55.0gr and bumping the shoulder back .001″ will net me an ICC average of 54.0gr. LAPUA runs an average of 54.4gr and Federal runs an average of 54.3gr ICC.”

cases.measurementMethod: TABLE ONE - Case Capacity Comparison (German Salazar). Internal capacity of Remington 22-250, Winchester 22-250, Norma 22-250, Norma 6XC and Tubb (3rd Generation) brass (all after fire-forming) is very close, allowing safe interchange of load data between these brass types. However, first Generation Tubb brass is very heavy (approx. 172 grains) and has much less case capacity - it is not suitable for the loads discussed in this article. I have not been able to locate any Tubb 2nd Generation brass for measurement.

cases.measurementMethod: Reader report quoted in prose (method, fill point and sample size not stated).
cases.evidence: The most important thing to remember about military brass is that the internal capacity will probably be less than commercial .308 Win brass, because military brass often has thicker webs or casewalls. Montana Marine reports his fire-formed milsurp cases hold 56 grains of H20 on average compared to 58 grains for fire-formed Winchester. Given the reduced capacity of military brass, you should reduce posted max loads by 1.5 grains when loading with Lake City or most other milsurp brass. However, the IMI MATCH brass is closer to commercial brass in internal case capacity (ICC). Kevin Beggs reports: “Fired, my IMI Match brass runs with an ICC of 55.0gr and bumping the shoulder back .001″ will net me an ICC average of 54.0gr. LAPUA runs an average of 54.4gr and Federal runs an average of 54.3gr ICC.”
cases.notes: Reader "Montana Marine" report quoted by AccurateShooter; average of his fire-formed cases. Same report: his fire-formed military-surplus cases (no single headstamp) hold the first value on average.

cases.measurementMethod: Reader report quoted in prose (method, fill point and sample size not stated).
cases.evidence: The most important thing to remember about military brass is that the internal capacity will probably be less than commercial .308 Win brass, because military brass often has thicker webs or casewalls. Montana Marine reports his fire-formed milsurp cases hold 56 grains of H20 on average compared to 58 grains for fire-formed Winchester. Given the reduced capacity of military brass, you should reduce posted max loads by 1.5 grains when loading with Lake City or most other milsurp brass. However, the IMI MATCH brass is closer to commercial brass in internal case capacity (ICC).
